Equipment and Gear for Cricket We've created a checklist for you with everything that you need to play cricket on a regular basis and on a more serious level! So you've just started playing the game more seriously, you may or may not have got the gear and equipment yet but you're wondering if there's anything else you need to add? Here's a checklist for you to be sure that you've got it all ready. You literally just need two things to begin the game:1. BallAny softball- mostly soft tennis ball/ Hard Tennis ball2. BatBasic Bat - Plastic bats/ Poplar / Poplar Willow If you wish to play on a more performance level, you'll need the right gear and equipment regulated by the laws of cricket. Here's a list that could help you begin.1. BallOn a performance level, the ball usually used in cricket is a cork ball covered in leather. In terms of color, there are two. Red balls used in Test Cricket and for First Class Cricket while white is used in one-day matches. Be on guard because these balls are very hard and can cause injuries upon impact with the body. 2. BatCricket Bats are made of flat wood not longer than 96.5cm. The width of these bats is restricted to 10.8cm. While there is no standard weight, most bats range from 1.2 kilograms to 1.4 kilograms. A white polo t-shirt is required for every Cricket Match. In the colder seasons, long-sleeved polo t-shirt is also sometimes worn. This is usually paired with white long trousers.Headwear that includes baseball caps or cricket caps/ sun caps is also recommended. For shoes, wear spiked shoes in order to improve traction on the playing area. Like every other sport, protective gear is absolutely required to ensure safety and stay injury-free. Batters and Wicketkeepers wear an abdomen guard to protect themselves from the impact of the ball hitting their body. Leg pads or shin pads are commonly worn by batters, wicketkeepers as well as the fielders stationed near the batter. A helmet, sometimes with an attached visor is worn by batters and fielders to protect their head. It is recommended for wicketkeepers to wear protective eyewear as well. The impacts of the ball hitting the wicket can be major with the bails getting dislodged after the impact. Batters and Wicketkeeper have different gloves. The ones worn by batters are very thickly padded at the tip of all five fingers when it's compared to thinner wicketkeeping gloves. The wicketkeeper gloves have webbed fingers to help catch the ball.
